passages.text: There is another evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily upon mankind: God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires; but God does not allow him to enjoy them. Instead, a stranger will enjoy them. This is futile and a grievous affliction.
passages.sermon:
I have seen another evil under the sun.
This evil is very great for mankind.
God gives a man riches.
God gives him wealth.
God gives him honor.
This man lacks nothing that he desires.
But God does not let him enjoy these things.
A stranger will enjoy them instead.
This is meaningless.
This is a grievous affliction.
passages.original: יֵ֣שׁ רָעָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר רָאִ֖יתִי תַּ֣חַת הַשָּׁ֑מֶשׁ וְרַבָּ֥ה הִ֖יא עַל־ הָאָדָֽם׃ אִ֣ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִתֶּן־ ל֣וֹ הָאֱלֹהִ֡ים עֹשֶׁר֩ וּנְכָסִ֨ים וְכָב֜וֹד וְֽאֵינֶ֨נּוּ חָסֵ֥ר לְנַפְשׁ֣וֹ׀ מִכֹּ֣ל אֲשֶׁר־ יִתְאַוֶּ֗ה וְלֹֽא־ יַשְׁלִיטֶ֤נּוּ הָֽאֱלֹהִים֙ לֶאֱכֹ֣ל מִמֶּ֔נּוּ כִּ֛י אִ֥ישׁ נָכְרִ֖י יֹֽאכֲלֶ֑נּוּ זֶ֥ה הֶ֛בֶל וָחֳלִ֥י רָ֖ע הֽוּא׃

passages.text: A man may father a hundred children and live for many years; yet no matter how long he lives, if he is unsatisfied with his prosperity and does not even receive a proper burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.
passages.sermon:
A man may have a hundred children.
He may live for many years.
His days may be very long.
But if he is not satisfied with good things,
and if he does not receive a proper burial,
then a stillborn child is better off than he.
passages.original: אִם־ יוֹלִ֣יד אִ֣ישׁ מֵאָ֡ה וְשָׁנִים֩ רַבּ֨וֹת יִֽחְיֶ֜ה וְרַ֣ב׀ שֶׁיִּהְי֣וּ יְמֵֽי־ שָׁנָ֗יו וְנַפְשׁוֹ֙ לֹא־ תִשְׂבַּ֣ע מִן־ הַטּוֹבָ֔ה וְגַם־ קְבוּרָ֖ה לֹא־ הָ֣יְתָה לּ֑וֹ אָמַ֕רְתִּי ט֥וֹב מִמֶּ֖נּוּ הַנָּֽפֶל׃

passages.text: For a stillborn child enters in futility and departs in darkness, and his name is shrouded in obscurity.
passages.sermon:
A stillborn child enters life in futility.
The child departs in darkness.
People cover the child’s name in darkness.
No one remembers the child’s name.
passages.original: כִּֽי־ בַהֶ֥בֶל בָּ֖א וּבַחֹ֣שֶׁךְ יֵלֵ֑ךְ וּבַחֹ֖שֶׁךְ שְׁמ֥וֹ יְכֻסֶּֽה׃

passages.text: The child, though neither seeing the sun nor knowing anything, has more rest than that man, even if he lives a thousand years twice over but fails to enjoy his prosperity. Do not all go to the same place?
passages.sermon:
A stillborn child does not see the sun.
A stillborn child does not know anything.
A stillborn child has more rest than a man who is never satisfied.
A man may live two thousand years.
A man may never enjoy good things.
Everyone goes to the same place in the end.
passages.original: גַּם־ שֶׁ֥מֶשׁ לֹא־ רָאָ֖ה וְלֹ֣א יָדָ֑ע נַ֥חַת לָזֶ֖ה מִזֶּֽה׃ וְאִלּ֣וּ חָיָ֗ה אֶ֤לֶף שָׁנִים֙ פַּעֲמַ֔יִם וְטוֹבָ֖ה לֹ֣א רָאָ֑ה הֲלֹ֛א אֶל־ מָק֥וֹם אֶחָ֖ד הַכֹּ֥ל הוֹלֵֽךְ׃

passages.text: All a man’s labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied.
passages.sermon:
A man works hard to feed himself.
He labors to satisfy his hunger.
But his soul is never filled.
His appetite is never satisfied.
passages.original: כָּל־ עֲמַ֥ל הָאָדָ֖ם לְפִ֑יהוּ וְגַם־ הַנֶּ֖פֶשׁ לֹ֥א תִמָּלֵֽא׃

passages.text: What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool? What gain comes to the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others?
passages.sermon:
A wise man uses knowledge and understanding.
A fool lacks wisdom and understanding.
The wise man and the fool both live in the world.
The wise man does not have a true advantage over the fool.
A poor man may know how to behave among people.
The poor man gains nothing lasting from this knowledge.
No one gains true profit from wisdom or skill alone.
passages.original: כִּ֛י מַה־ יּוֹתֵ֥ר לֶחָכָ֖ם מִֽן־ הַכְּסִ֑יל מַה־ לֶּעָנִ֣י יוֹדֵ֔עַ לַהֲלֹ֖ךְ נֶ֥גֶד הַחַיִּֽים׃

passages.text: Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
passages.sermon:
The writer of Ecclesiastes speaks about human desire and satisfaction.
He says it is better to have what you can see.
It is better to have what is in front of you.
It is better than chasing after what you want but do not have.
Chasing after desire is empty.
This is also pointless.
It is like trying to catch the wind.
passages.original: ט֛וֹב מַרְאֵ֥ה עֵינַ֖יִם מֵֽהֲלָךְ־ נָ֑פֶשׁ גַּם־ זֶ֥ה הֶ֖בֶל וּרְע֥וּת רֽוּחַ׃

passages.text: Whatever exists was named long ago, and what happens to a man is foreknown; but he cannot contend with one stronger than he.
passages.sermon:
God knows everything that exists.
God gave each thing its name long ago.
God knows what will happen to every person.
A person is only a human being.
A person cannot argue with God.
God is stronger than any person.
passages.original: מַה־ שֶּֽׁהָיָ֗ה כְּבָר֙ נִקְרָ֣א שְׁמ֔וֹ וְנוֹדָ֖ע אֲשֶׁר־ ה֣וּא אָדָ֑ם וְלֹא־ יוּכַ֣ל לָדִ֔ין עִ֥ם שֶׁהַתְקִיף מִמֶּֽנּוּ׃

passages.text: For the more words, the more futility—and how does that profit anyone?
passages.sermon:
Many words exist.
Many words increase futility.
Futility means something is useless.
More words do not help a person.
More words do not give anyone profit.
passages.original: כִּ֛י יֵשׁ־ דְּבָרִ֥ים הַרְבֵּ֖ה מַרְבִּ֣ים הָ֑בֶל מַה־ יֹּתֵ֖ר לָאָדָֽם׃

passages.text: For who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow? Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?
passages.sermon:
A man lives only a short time.
His life passes quickly, like a shadow.
No one truly knows what is good for a man in this life.
No one can tell a man what will happen after he is gone.
No one knows what will come after him on earth.
passages.original: כִּ֣י מִֽי־ יוֹדֵעַ֩ מַה־ טּ֨וֹב לָֽאָדָ֜ם בַּֽחַיִּ֗ים מִסְפַּ֛ר יְמֵי־ חַיֵּ֥י הֶבְל֖וֹ וְיַעֲשֵׂ֣ם כַּצֵּ֑ל אֲשֶׁר֙ מִֽי־ יַגִּ֣יד לָֽאָדָ֔ם מַה־ יִּהְיֶ֥ה אַחֲרָ֖יו תַּ֥חַת הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ׃
